claims.claim: The multiplicity of DnaK-substrate conformations should be a common characteristic of Hsp70-client complexes in general.
claims.source: The conserved topology of the substrate binding site suggests that the multiplicity of DnaK-substrate conformations observed presently should be a common characteristic of Hsp70-client complexes in general.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the binding site.

claims.claim: At least four peaks for Ile 29 are observed in the presence of Hsc70, demonstrating the existence of conformational heterogeneity in the Hsc70-hTRF1 complex.
claims.source: In order to verify this we recorded HMQC spectra of a sample of ILVM-13CH3 hTRF1 containing a two-fold excess of human U-2H Hsc70/ADP (Figure 6). The Ile region of this spectrum clearly shows at least four peaks for Ile 29 in the presence of Hsc70, demonstrating the existence of conformational heterogeneity in the Hsc70-hTRF1 complex as well.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Three-helix bundle proteins represent ~10% of all in vivo substrates interacting with E.coli DnaK.
claims.source: Three-helix bundle proteins have previously been shown to represent ~10% of all in vivo substrates interacting with E.coli DnaK (Calloni et al., 2012); in addition, conformational heterogeneity has also been detected in the binding of a β-sheet protein with DnaK (Lee et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The promiscuity of Hsp70 and the heterogeneous nature of Hsp70-client complexes are general features.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the promiscuity of Hsp70 and the heterogeneous nature of Hsp70-client complexes are general features, beyond what has been characterized in detail in the present study of the DnaK-hTRF1 complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and comparison to other studies.

claims.claim: The residues that are part of the DnaK binding pocket are inherently malleable so that DnaK can recognize and bind to at least four different sites on hTRF1.
claims.source: We find that the residues that are part of the DnaK binding pocket are inherently malleable so that DnaK can recognize and bind to at least four different sites on the small 6 kDa, 53 residue hTRF1 substrate that have been characterized in the present work.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing multiple binding sites and rotamer flexibility.

claims.claim: DnaK will likely bind to multiple client sites on typical client proteins that are much larger than 53 residues.
claims.source: Since typical client proteins of DnaK are much larger than 53 residues, it is very likely that DnaK will bind to multiple client sites, generally.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of multiple binding sites on a small substrate.

claims.claim: Binding of Hsp70 at different positions creates sub-ensembles with distinct conformational preferences and different starting structures for folding upon release.
claims.source: Our results, therefore suggest a model for Hsp70-mediated conformational biasing whereby binding of Hsp70 at different positions of a substrate creates sub-ensembles with distinct conformational preferences and hence different starting structures for folding upon release from Hsp70, thereby broadening the conformational space sampled by the substrate as it folds.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The DnaK-hTRF1 ensemble is a fuzzy complex, characterized by both static and dynamic disorder.
claims.source: More generally, our study establishes that the DnaK-hTRF1 ensemble is a fuzzy complex, characterized by both static and dynamic disorder.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple conformations and conformational dynamics.

claims.claim: The heterogeneity resulting from Hsp70 binding enables the client protein to explore a number of starting conformations as a means for navigating kinetic traps in the conformational free energy landscape.
claims.source: The heterogeneity resulting from Hsp70 binding thus enables the client protein to explore a number of starting conformations, that lead to the formation of different amounts and types of local structure, as a means for navigating kinetic traps in the conformational free energy landscape and for promoting efficient folding to the native state.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Such a mechanism of Hsp70 function is expected to be particularly beneficial for proteins with rugged free energy landscapes and local minima that trap misfolded and aggregation-prone conformations.
claims.source: Such a mechanism of Hsp70 function is expected to be particularly beneficial for proteins with rugged free energy landscapes and local minima that trap misfolded and aggregation-prone conformations, where folding yield is increased by recycling kinetically trapped molecules at the expense of a decrease in folding rate resulting from repeated binding to the Hsp70 chaperone (Agashe et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Slower folding in the presence of the Hsp70 chaperone system has been observed for RNase H.
claims.source: Slower folding in the presence of the Hsp70 chaperone system has indeed been observed in the literature for RNase H (Sekhar et al., 2012a), though such a decrease is predicted to be negligible for fast-folding proteins like hTRF1 (56) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation and simulations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The chaperone-substrate interaction studied here adds to the increasing number of examples of conformational heterogeneity observed in concert with molecular recognition.
claims.source: The chaperone-substrate interaction studied here adds to the increasing number of examples of conformational heterogeneity observed in concert with molecular recognition (Boehr et al., 2009; Mittag et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on conformational heterogeneity in molecular recognition.

claims.claim: In the DnaK-hTRF1 complex, the multiplicity of Hsp70 client binding modes leads to static disorder at the binding interface.
claims.source: In the present case the multiplicity of Hsp70 client binding modes leads to static disorder at the binding interface, where each sub-ensemble has a well-defined structure, with dissociation and subsequent re-association of the substrate occurring on a slow timescale.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple conformations with slow exchange.

claims.claim: Parts of the substrate polypeptide chain distal to the Hsp70 binding site are globally unfolded with local secondary structure, resulting in rapidly interconverting states and dynamic disorder.
claims.source: We have shown earlier that parts of the substrate polypeptide chain distal to the Hsp70 binding site are globally unfolded with local secondary structure (Sekhar et al., 2015, 2016), resulting in rapidly interconverting states and dynamic disorder in these regions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The DnaK-hTRF1 complex is a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder that enhances exploration of the free energy landscape.
claims.source: Such a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder enhances exploration of the free energy landscape, facilitating the efficient folding of the substrate to its native conformation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and their functional implications.

claims.claim: The model proposed for Hsp70-mediated protein folding is broadly similar to that proposed for GroEL/ES function.
claims.source: The model proposed above for Hsp70-mediated protein folding is broadly similar to that proposed for GroEL/ES function, wherein GroEL/ES maintains kinetically trapped conformers in a globally unfolded state and subsequently releases them for folding (Weissman et al., 1994; Todd et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to another chaperone system, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the case of Hsp70, the starting conformation for substrate folding can potentially be different in every binding cycle.
claims.source: However, in the case of Hsp70 the starting conformation for substrate folding can potentially be different in every binding cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of multiple binding sites.

claims.claim: Hsp70-mediated folding does not rely passively on stochastic refolding from the same conformation, but instead actively alters starting structures as a strategy to sample different folding pathways.
claims.source: Therefore, Hsp70-mediated folding does not rely passively on stochastic refolding from the same conformation, but instead actively alters starting structures as a strategy to sample a different folding pathway and hence different regions of conformational space during each iteration.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The presence of multiple chaperone interaction sites on the substrate is a feature shared between Hsp70, SecB and trigger factor.
claims.source: The presence of multiple chaperone interaction sites on the substrate is a feature shared between Hsp70, SecB (Lilly et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2016) and trigger factor (Saio et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on other chaperones.

claims.claim: SecB and trigger factor utilize several surface-exposed hydrophobic pockets for capturing substrate molecules, resulting in a complex where the substrate wraps around the chaperone and buries 4000–8000 Å2 of surface area at the interface.
claims.source: However, SecB and trigger factor utilize several surface-exposed hydrophobic pockets for capturing substrate molecules, resulting in a complex where the substrate wraps around the chaperone and buries 4000–8000 Å2 of surface area at the interface (Lilly et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2016; Saio et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of SecB and trigger factor.

claims.claim: Hsp70 interacts with substrates using predominantly one binding site that contacts the substrate minimally at 4–5 residues, allowing the rest of the chain to explore conformational space.
claims.source: In contrast, Hsp70 interacts with substrates using predominantly one binding site (though interactions with the α-helical lid have been observed previously [Smock et al., 2011]) that contacts the substrate minimally at 4–5 residues, allowing the rest of the chain to explore conformational space.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from structural knowledge and the experimental observations, with a citation.

claims.claim: The mechanism of Hsp70 action is different from those of SecB and trigger factor and appears to be tailored towards its function in assisting protein folding.
claims.source: The mechanism of Hsp70 action is thus different from those of SecB and trigger factor and appears to be tailored towards its function in assisting protein folding.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the mechanisms of different chaperones.

claims.claim: The DnaK-hTRF1 interaction is a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder.
claims.source: In the present case the multiplicity of Hsp70 client binding modes leads to static disorder at the binding interface, where each sub-ensemble has a well-defined structure, with dissociation and subsequent re-association of the substrate occurring on a slow timescale. We have shown earlier that parts of the substrate polypeptide chain distal to the Hsp70 binding site are globally unfolded with local secondary structure (Sekhar et al., 2015, 2016), resulting in rapidly interconverting states and dynamic disorder in these regions. Such a fuzzy complex with static and dynamic disorder enhances exploration of the free energy landscape, facilitating the efficient folding of the substrate to its native conformation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of multiple conformations and conformational dynamics.

claims.claim: Large proteins like luciferase are expected to have several kinetic traps in their folding free energy landscape.
claims.source: Large proteins like luciferase are expected to have several kinetic traps in their folding free energy landscape; in the first binding cycle it is conceivable that only a few sub-ensembles of Hsp70-bound luciferase lead to starting conformations for the client upon release that bypass these kinetic traps and result in efficient folding.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the folding behavior of large proteins based on the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: The net probability of folding and hence the folding efficiency increases with the number of iterations that a substrate undergoes through the chaperone cycle.
claims.source: Since only a fraction of folding-competent conformations are generated during any particular iteration of the Hsp70 chaperone cycle, it follows that the net probability of folding and hence the folding efficiency increases with the number of iterations that a substrate undergoes through the chaperone cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: Substrate proteins typically undergo multiple rounds of binding and release before folding to the native state.
claims.source: Our data provides a rationale for why substrate proteins typically undergo multiple rounds of binding and release before folding to the native state (Mayer, 2013; Szabo et al., 1994; Clerico et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and explained by the proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: DnaK may be able to bind to the SH3 domain in different ways.
claims.source: Our work also sheds light into the cause of the conformational heterogeneity that was previously reported for a complex between the N-terminal SH3 domain from Drk and DnaK based on the observation of multiple peaks for specific residues in a 1H-15N HSQC spectrum of the complex (Lee et al., 2015). While the origin of the peaks was unclear in that study it now appears that DnaK may be able to bind to the SH3 domain in different ways.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and a previous study cited.

claims.claim: Multiple modes of binding, including the existence of forward and reverse modes and registry shifts, have been seen in crystal structures of short peptides with DnaK.
claims.source: Multiple modes of binding, including the existence of forward and reverse modes and registry shifts, have also been seen in crystal structures of short peptides with DnaK (Zahn et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to crystal structures.

claims.claim: Multiple binding modes can exist at equilibrium in solution.
claims.source: Here we establish that such multiple binding modes can exist at equilibrium in solution and we elucidate the molecular determinants for the formation of a heterogeneous chaperone-substrate ensemble.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in solution.

results.result: DnaK binds to at least four distinct sites on hTRF1 (Leu 30, Leu 31, Val 18, and Val 41), as demonstrated by methyl-TROSY NMR spectroscopy showing multiple conformations of the DnaK-hTRF1 complex. These binding sites were identified through mutagenesis experiments and NOESY data linking specific hTRF1 residues to DnaK binding pocket residues Ile 401 and Ile 438.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C23-C24, C31-C36 provide converging experimental evidence from NMR spectroscopy (multiple peaks for Ile 29), diffusion measurements confirming bound states, NOESY data linking substrate and chaperone residues, and mutagenesis experiments definitively assigning four binding sites. The data is internally consistent and well-supported by multiple independent experimental approaches.

results.result: A fraction of hTRF1 molecules bind two DnaK molecules simultaneously, with the 'c' state (Val 41 at position 0) showing 2:1 DnaK:hTRF1 stoichiometry based on NMR titration data, while states 'a', 'b', and 'd' show 1:1 stoichiometry. This demonstrates that even a small 53-residue substrate can accommodate multiple chaperone molecules at equilibrium.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C38-C39, C41 are supported by systematic NMR titration experiments showing distinct maxima at different [DnaK]T/[hTRF1]T ratios (1:1 for states a, b, d and 2:1 for state c). The interpretation is validated by mathematical modeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) demonstrating that these titration profiles are consistent with the proposed stoichiometries.

results.result: The DnaK binding pocket exhibits considerable flexibility, with Ile 401 and Ile 438 rotamer distributions varying substantially across different bound conformations. The binding pocket topology is influenced not only by the identity of the substrate residue at position 0 but also by other factors, as evidenced by different rotamer populations for states 'a' and 'b' despite both having Leu at position 0.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by quantitative analysis of 13C chemical shifts (Table 1) showing rotamer distributions ranging from 42-99% gauche- for Ile 401 and 0-100% for Ile 438. The observation that Ile 438 trans population changes from 28% to 54% between states 'a' and 'b' (both with Leu at position 0) provides direct evidence that factors beyond residue identity govern binding pocket topology.

results.result: The interconversion between multiple DnaK-bound states is slow, with substrate off-rate (koff) less than 0.3 s⁻¹, as determined by magnetization exchange experiments showing no exchange crosspeaks at 300 ms mixing time. This is consistent with previously measured slow substrate release rates from DnaK/ADP (~0.001 s⁻¹ at 25°C).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by direct experimental evidence (absence of exchange crosspeaks in magnetization exchange experiments) and simulations establishing the upper limit for koff. The consistency with previously published kinetic measurements strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Multiple DnaK-bound conformations are observed with peptide fragments (hTRF1₂₃₋₃₈ and hTRF1₃₄₋₄₉) and with DnaK/ATP (where the lid is less interactive), demonstrating that conformational heterogeneity does not require the full-length substrate or specific lid-substrate interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by experimental data showing multiple peaks in HMQC spectra for both peptide-DnaK complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and DnaK/ATP-hTRF1 complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). These control experiments effectively rule out alternative explanations for the observed heterogeneity.

results.result: The relative binding affinities of the three 1:1 complexes differ, with Kd ratios of 1:2.6:20.1 for states 'a':'b':'d' (corresponding to free energy differences of 0:0.6:1.8 kcal/mol at 35°C), as estimated from peak intensity ratios at [DnaK]T/[hTRF1]T = 1.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 provides quantitative binding affinity estimates based on peak intensities. However, the authors acknowledge this is only approximate due to potential differential relaxation effects (13% maximum variation noted). While 1H and 13C linewidths are reported as similar, the assumption that intensities directly reflect concentrations may introduce systematic errors. The relative trends are likely valid, but absolute values should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: Conformational heterogeneity in Hsp70-client complexes is a general feature, as demonstrated by similar multiple conformations observed with human Hsc70 binding to hTRF1. The conserved topology of the substrate binding site across the Hsp70 family suggests this promiscuity is widespread.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C47, C50 are supported by experimental data showing at least four peaks for Ile 29 in Hsc70-hTRF1 complexes (Figure 6), combined with structural conservation arguments and citations to studies showing heterogeneity with other substrates (β-sheet proteins). The generalization is appropriately cautious and evidence-based.

results.result: This is the first study demonstrating that a Val residue can occupy the central (0) position in a DnaK-substrate complex, expanding the known repertoire of residues that can bind in the central pocket beyond Ile, Leu, Met, Pro, and cyclohexylalanine.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by the mutagenesis and labeling experiments definitively assigning Val 18 and Val 41 to positions 0 in states 'd' and 'c'. The novelty claim is appropriately qualified ('to the best of our knowledge') and contextualized with citations to known binding residues.

results.result: The DnaK-hTRF1 complex is a 'fuzzy complex' characterized by static disorder (multiple binding modes with slow exchange) and dynamic disorder (rapidly interconverting states in regions distal to binding site). This heterogeneity enables substrate molecules to explore different starting conformations upon release, potentially allowing them to circumvent kinetic traps and sample different folding pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C53-C55, C61, C64 present a mechanistic model based on the experimental observations. While the characterization of the complex as 'fuzzy' with static and dynamic disorder is well-supported by data (C54, C59-C60, C69), the functional implications (C53, C55, C61, C64) regarding kinetic trap avoidance and folding pathway sampling are speculative inferences. The model is plausible and consistent with the data, but lacks direct experimental validation of the proposed folding mechanism.

results.result: The proposed mechanism is expected to be particularly beneficial for proteins with rugged energy landscapes, where multiple binding cycles increase folding efficiency. Slower folding with Hsp70 has been observed for some proteins (RNase H) but is predicted to be negligible for fast-folding proteins like hTRF1.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C70-C72 extend the mechanistic model to make predictions about different protein classes. While C57 provides supporting evidence from literature and simulations for hTRF1, the broader predictions (C56, C70-C71) remain speculative. The logic is sound and the model is testable, but experimental validation for proteins with rugged landscapes is needed.

results.result: The Hsp70 mechanism differs from GroEL/ES and other chaperones (SecB, trigger factor) in that Hsp70 can generate different starting conformations in each binding cycle through promiscuous binding, while using minimal substrate contacts (4-5 residues) that allow conformational exploration, rather than extensive wrapping around the chaperone.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C65-C68 make comparative mechanistic arguments supported by citations to structural and functional studies of other chaperones. The distinction between Hsp70's minimal contact strategy versus the extensive wrapping by SecB/trigger factor is well-established in the literature. The inference that this enables different functional mechanisms is logical and appropriately qualified.

results.result: Methyl-TROSY NMR spectroscopy enabled detection of residues at the DnaK binding site (residues 27-39) that were invisible in conventional 1H-15N TROSY experiments due to slow tumbling of the ~80 kDa complex and conformational heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 describe the methodological approach and its rationale. The limitation of 1H-15N experiments is documented (C21), and the advantages of methyl-TROSY are well-established in the literature (C22). The successful detection of multiple conformations validates the approach.

results.result: Background context on Hsp70 function and structure: Hsp70 is critical for cellular proteostasis, performs diverse ATP-dependent functions, recognizes clients with broad conformational range, yet has a simple binding site architecture where peptides bind in extended conformations with minimal contacts. The binding pocket may possess considerable flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C7-C14 provide established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to previous structural and functional studies. These claims appropriately contextualize the study and identify the knowledge gap (C3) that the work addresses.

results.result: The model substrate hTRF1 is a marginally stable 53-residue three-helix bundle with one predicted strong DnaK binding site (Leu 31) and two weak sites. Previous studies showed DnaK-bound hTRF1 is globally unfolded but retains ~40% secondary structure in regions distal to the binding site, with disrupted tertiary interactions, and this conformation is maintained throughout the DnaK nucleotide cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 describe the substrate properties and previous findings, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work by the authors and others. This establishes the foundation for the current study.

results.result: The current findings provide insight into previously observed conformational heterogeneity in other DnaK-substrate complexes (SH3 domain) and establish that multiple binding modes observed in crystal structures can exist at equilibrium in solution.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 connect the current findings to previous observations in the literature. The inference that DnaK can bind the SH3 domain in different ways (C73) is reasonable given the current results, and the demonstration that crystal structure heterogeneity reflects solution equilibria (C75) is directly supported by the NMR data.
